rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, field plot experiment in Xinjiang 2021 with processing tomato, 2x2 factorial (aeration x N), three replicates. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3, aerated irrigation had highly significant effects on yield, yield components, IWUE and NPFP; A1N2 gave the highest yield (32.05 t/ha), 23.69% above A0N1, and A1N1 exceeded A0N1. Q4: Section 3.5 and Figure 8, path analysis modelling how fertilizer-air coupled drip irrigation alters soil nutrients (NO3-N, NH4-N, SOC, DOC) and C/N cycling gene abundance, which in turn directly affect yield; soil nutrients measured in Figure 4. Q9: Table 3 reports yield, IWUE and NPFP as mean <U+00B1> standard deviation for each treatment.
rows.notes: Only the yield/IWUE/NPFP part of the passage is supported; crop quality was not measured and 'excessive consumption of nutrient elements' is not directly tested (NPFP rose with aeration, but N uptake was not measured). Single site, single season, single crop and soil; harvest weighing is the only yield method. Soil oxygen/aeration itself was not measured; the mechanism of improved soil aeration/porosity is asserted citing Western et al. Statement that highest yield required aerated irrigation with 270 kg N is a recommendation/interaction rather than a stated requirement for the aeration effect, which occurred at both N levels. No limitations stated.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, own field experiment with processing tomato under aerated and non-aerated mulched drip irrigation.
rows.notes: The study contains no result on pesticide use or pest/disease incidence. Section 2.2 states that weeding and pesticide applications were applied uniformly across all plots as standard practice. It measured soil nutrients, GHG emissions, C/N cycling gene abundance and yield only, so it provides no evidence for reduced pesticide applications under ADI.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, field plot experiment in Xinjiang 2021, processing tomato, aeration x N factorial with three replicates. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3, aerated irrigation significantly increased single fruit weight, yield per plant, total yield, IWUE and NPFP (p<0.01); A1N2 yield 32.05 t/ha, 23.69% above A0N1. Q4: Section 3.5 and Figure 8, path analysis modelling the chain from air-fertilizer coupled drip irrigation through soil nutrients and C/N cycling genes to yield; soil nutrient contents measured in Figure 4. Q9: Table 3 gives yield, IWUE, NPFP and yield components as mean <U+00B1> SD.
rows.notes: Crop performance here is yield, yield components, IWUE and NPFP; aeration reduced number of fruits per plant. One site, one year, one crop; single measurement method; no soil oxygen measurement; no stated limitations; recommendations about moderate N and 450 mm irrigation are not framed as requirements for the aeration effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, own field experiment with 0-40 cm soil sampling at fruit expansion stage. Q2: Section 3.1 and Figure 4, aeration increased SOC and DOC by 1.75-10.94% and 3.21-3.30% and NH4-N by 7.75-14.44% relative to non-aerated drip; abstract and conclusion state aerated irrigation increased SOC, DOC, TN and NH4-N; Section 3.2 and Figure 5 report functional gene abundance responses. Q9: Figure 4 caption, bars represent standard deviation of the mean (n=3).
rows.notes: Evidence on soil condition is mixed: Section 3.1 also reports aeration reduced TN and NO3-N (by 11.39% and 20.00%), and Section 3.3 reports aeration increased N2O, CO2, CH4 and total GHG emissions, so 'improved soil condition' is only partly supported. Single sampling date, one site, one soil (sandy loam), one year; standard lab chemical analysis is the only method. Root-zone oxygen or soil aeration was not measured, mechanism asserted via citations. No limitations stated.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-site, single-season (2021) plot experiment with processing tomato under mulched drip irrigation, comparing Venturi-aerated vs non-aerated drip at two N rates. Abstract and conclusion inconsistently refer to the high N rate as 270 and 240 kg/ha.
